title: The Mandate Changes Hands
subtitle: The fall of the Ming and the Qing conquest: Beijing, Shanhai Pass, Yangzhou and Jiangnan, 1644–1646
intro: On 25 April 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng's army walked into Beijing and the last Ming emperor hanged himself behind the palace. Within six weeks the rebels were gone too: the Ming general Wu Sangui opened Shanhai Pass to the Manchus, the combined armies broke Li on 27 May, and the Qing regent Dorgon rode into the capital on 6 June. A year later Qing armies crossed the Yangtze. Yangzhou was sacked in May 1645, Nanjing surrendered in June, and the order to shave the head and wear the queue set Jiangnan on fire that summer. Jiangyin held out for some eighty days and fell in October.

The honest record of this cataclysm is not mostly diaries. Qi Biaojia's is the great exception, a daily diary kept by a Ming official for fifteen years and broken off only by his suicide in 1645. Around it this chapter sets other kinds of writing and says so: Wang Xiuchu's dated survivor's narrative of Yangzhou; the official diary kept by the Korean crown prince's retinue as they travelled with the conquering army; Shi Kefa's letters; Dorgon's edicts; the memoirs Adam Schall and Martino Martini compiled for Europe; Zhang Dai's memories written in hiding; and the Japanese shogunate's file of sailors' reports.

The eyes are deliberately unlike one another. A Manchu regent and a Ming commander write to each other. A German Jesuit stays in the captured capital and sells the new dynasty an accurate calendar. A Korean prince, hostage of the Qing and loyal in spirit to the Ming, enters Beijing behind Dorgon and dies at home the day after Yangzhou falls. A Yangzhou townsman counts his dead. Two Shaoxing friends choose death and survival. A Japanese scholar hears of it all five months late and names his file 'the transformation from civilised to barbarian'.

The Yangzhou entries are treated soberly. Wang's account is a primary witness, but it is also a text with a history: suppressed under the Qing, reprinted as revolutionary propaganda, and carrying a death toll of 800,000 that historians reject. The entries give what he recorded and how he survived, not the violence in detail.

Many of these writers recorded or remembered events after the fact. Where only the month or season is secure, the entry says so, and day-level content that could not be checked is described only in general terms. Read the dates as a weave of near and far: the same week looked very different from the observatory in Beijing, a garden in Shaoxing, a roof in Yangzhou, and an office in Edo.
calendar_note: Chinese, Korean and Japanese writers used the lunisolar calendar and reign years: Chongzhen 17 (1644) for the Ming, Shunzhi 1–3 (1644–46) for the Qing, Hongguang 1 (1645) for the Southern Ming court Qi and Shi served, Injo 22–23 for Joseon, and Shōhō 1–3 for Japan. Each entry's date_display gives the original reign date (e.g. Chongzhen 17, 3rd month, 19th day) and date_iso the Gregorian equivalent, which is the calendar the Jesuits Schall and Martini used. The conversions were made with an astronomical lunisolar algorithm and match the standard Gregorian dates for the key events (25 April 1644 for the fall of Beijing, 27 May for Shanhai Pass, 19 June for the Hongguang enthronement, 20 May 1645 for Yangzhou, 8 June 1645 for Nanjing). The Ming Datong calendar, the Qing calendar (from 1645 built on Schall's methods) and Joseon reckoning could differ by a day, which is why some events appear a day apart in modern books: the Qing entry into Beijing is given as 5 or 6 June, and the fall of Jiangyin as 9 or 10 October 1645. 1645 had an intercalary sixth month (late July to August), the month of Qi Biaojia's death.

eyes.name: Qi Biaojia (祁彪佳)
eyes.role: Ming scholar-official aged about 42; under the Southern Ming Hongguang court a senior regional official in Jiangnan, then retired to his garden estate
eyes.where: Shaoxing and his Yushan (Mount Yu) garden at Shanyin; on official duty in Jiangnan in 1644
eyes.vantage_label: Jiangnan official, then a retired gentleman waiting for the conquest to arrive
eyes.authenticity: A near-continuous diary of some 400,000 characters running from Chongzhen 4 (1631) to his death in 1645, with a gap for his years as a censor in Suzhou–Songjiang; the final volume is the 'Yiyou rili' (Diary of 1645). Modern edition: Qi Biaojia riji, ed. Zhang Tianjie (Zhejiang Guji, 2017). Not translated into English as a whole. The day-level content of his 1644 entries is given here only in general terms; sources disagree on the exact date and setting of his death.
eyes.bio: A wealthy Shaoxing official, garden builder and drama connoisseur whose diary records famine relief, meditation, garden work and politics for fifteen years. It is the rare case of a Ming official writing day by day through the whole collapse, from the news of the capital's fall to the night he walked into his garden pond rather than serve the Qing. His friend Zhang Dai wrote from the same city, but in memory, not in a diary.

sources.title: Zhang Tianjie, essay on the Qi Biaojia riji (diary span 1631–1645; vol. 15 'Yiyou rili')
Lin Zhu, 'Poetics and politics of withdrawal' (Edinburgh PhD, 2021): Qi's garden and death
CBDB person record 33172

eyes.name: Wang Xiuchu (王秀楚)
eyes.role: A townsman of Yangzhou, otherwise unknown; head of an extended household
eyes.where: Inside Yangzhou, hiding with his family through the sack
eyes.vantage_label: direct victim inside the sacked city
eyes.form: dated eyewitness narrative (written after the events)
eyes.authenticity: 'Yangzhou shiri ji' (A Record of Ten Days in Yangzhou) is a retrospective first-person narrative arranged by lunar date, written by a survivor soon after. It was not printed under the Qing; copies survived (some in Japan) and anti-Qing writers republished it before the Taiping and 1911 revolutions. Its figure of 800,000 dead is regarded by historians as a great exaggeration. English translations: Backhouse and Bland; Lucien Mao; Lynn Struve (1998).
eyes.bio: Wang is known only from this text. He was no official and no soldier: his account is of hiding places, bribes, lost relatives and luck, including a Manchu officer who finally spared his family. Historians use it to confirm Shi Kefa's death; readers since the 1900s have used it as a symbol, which is part of its history.

sources.title: Yangzhou shiri ji, Chinese text with English notes (East Asia Student series)
Wang Xiuchu (Wikipedia)
Lynn Struve, Voices from the Ming–Qing Cataclysm (Yale, 1998)

eyes.name: Shi Kefa (史可法)
eyes.role: Minister of War of the Southern Ming Hongguang court and commander of the Huai–Yangzhou front, aged 42–43
eyes.where: Nanjing, then the Yangzhou front north of the Yangtze
eyes.authenticity: His reply to Dorgon's 1644 demand for submission is preserved in his collected writings and widely anthologised; farewell letters to his family from the siege also survive in his collected works. Exact days of composition are not secure here, so these entries are month-level.
eyes.bio: The Ming's most revered loyalist commander, who failed to hold together quarrelling generals north of the Yangtze. His letters are public performances of loyalty as well as private farewells, and he became the hero of Yangzhou's memory; Wang Xiuchu's account is the main witness to his end.

sources.title: Shi Kefa (Wikipedia; 'Reply to Dorgon's letter', death 20 May 1645)

eyes.name: Dorgon, Prince Rui (多爾袞)
eyes.role: Manchu prince and regent for the child Shunzhi Emperor, aged 32; commander of the 1644 campaign
eyes.authenticity: Not a diarist. His voice survives in edicts, proclamations and letters preserved in the Qing Veritable Records and anthologies; translated selections exist (e.g. the two edicts on hair). Included for contrast with the diarists, with dates at month precision where the exact day was not verified.
eyes.bio: The man who turned a Ming general's appeal for help into a change of dynasty. His orders, on mourning the dead Ming emperor, on submission and above all on shaving the head, are the events many of the other eyes are reacting to.

sources.title: Regent Dorgon: Two Edicts concerning the Wearing of Hair under Manchu Rule (1644–1645)
Battle of Shanhai Pass (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Crown Prince Sohyeon (昭顯世子) and his household diarists
eyes.role: Heir to the Joseon throne, aged 32, a hostage of the Qing since 1637; the diary was kept by officials of his tutorial office (Sigangwon)
eyes.side: Joseon Korea (tributary hostage of the Qing)
eyes.where: Shenyang; with the Qing army on the road to Beijing; Beijing; finally Seoul
eyes.vantage_label: unwilling guest in the conquering army's train
eyes.authenticity: 'Simyang ilgi' (Shenyang Diary), the office diary of the prince's retinue, survives in two Kyujanggak manuscript sets (a 10-volume draft in cursive and an 8-volume fair copy), covering 1637–1644. A separate one-volume 'Bukhaeng ilgi' (Diary of the Northern Journey) covers the 4th–6th lunar months of 1644, and a one-volume household diary covers 1645. Fully translated into Korean by a Kyujanggak team. The prince is the subject rather than the author. Day-level 1644 details below are dated from the Qing campaign chronology and marked approximate.
eyes.bio: Eight years a hostage, Sohyeon learned Manchu power from the inside and was taken along when Dorgon marched on Beijing. There he met Adam Schall and took home Western books and instruments. He died weeks after returning to Seoul, a death long suspected as poisoning. His household diary is the only daily record here written from inside the conquering column, by men who were neither Ming nor Qing.

sources.title: Simyang ilgi, Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (AKS)
Kyeonggi Ilbo on the four Sohyeon diaries and their translation
Au Tak Wai, A study on Sohyeon Simyang ilgi (HKU MPhil, 2021)
Crown Prince Sohyeon (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Johann Adam Schall von Bell
eyes.role: German Jesuit astronomer aged 52, long employed on the Ming calendar reform
eyes.side: Society of Jesus (Catholic mission in Beijing)
eyes.where: His church and residence inside Beijing
eyes.vantage_label: foreigner who stayed inside the captured capital
eyes.authenticity: His 'Historica narratio' (Vienna, 1665; expanded 'Historica relatio', Regensburg 1672) was assembled largely from his correspondence with Europe; both editions are incomplete, and a French translation by P. Bornet appeared in 1942. Written and edited later, with an interest in showing the mission's survival in a good light.
eyes.bio: Schall refused his superiors' advice to flee, stayed through the rebel occupation, refused again to leave when the Manchus cleared his quarter, and then offered his science to the new dynasty. Within months he had won an eclipse contest and a mandarin's rank. He is the hinge between Beijing's catastrophe and the Qing's quick claim to Heaven's calendar.

sources.title: Schall von Bell, Adam (Deutsche Biographie: NDB/ADB)
A Jesuit Astronomer in a Qing Emperor's Court (Chinese PEN)

eyes.name: Martino Martini
eyes.role: Italian Jesuit aged about 30, in China since 1643
eyes.side: Society of Jesus; served the Southern Ming, then accepted the Qing
eyes.where: Hangzhou; Wenzhou during the Qing advance into Zhejiang
eyes.vantage_label: European in the path of the conquest in Zhejiang
eyes.authenticity: 'De bello Tartarico historia' (Antwerp, 1654), reprinted about 25 times in five languages by 1706; an expanded 'Regni Sinensis a Tartaris devastati enarratio' followed in 1661. Mixes what he saw in Jiangsu and Zhejiang with friends' letters and hearsay, contradicts itself in places, and often diverges from modern reconstructions. His own Wenzhou episode appears in some editions.
eyes.bio: The man who told Europe about the Manchu conquest. He served the Southern Ming Longwu court, survived the fall of Wenzhou by turning his lodging into a display of European learning, shaved his head in the Manchu style, and was sent back to Hangzhou under Qing protection. His book made the war a European bestseller within a decade.

sources.title: Martino Martini (Wikipedia)
The Beijing Center: Eyewitness to the fall of the Ming dynasty (library tour)

eyes.name: Zhang Dai (張岱)
eyes.role: Shaoxing gentleman, essayist and historian, aged 47 in 1644
eyes.where: Shaoxing; briefly with the resistance there; then in hiding in the hills to the south

waypoints.label: Hiding in hills south of Shaoxing, 1646–

eyes.vantage_label: ruined aesthete remembering a vanished world
eyes.authenticity: 'Tao'an mengyi' (Dream Memories of Tao'an) was probably completed around 1647, while he was in hiding, and first printed (incomplete) in 1775. These are undated vignettes recalled after the fall, not a diary; dates here come from his own internal references and from Jonathan Spence's reconstruction.
eyes.bio: A rich man's son turned penniless refugee who wrote the most loved memoir of late-Ming pleasures, lanterns, tea, theatre, gardens, in the knowledge that all of it was gone. He was a friend of Qi Biaojia. His angle is the opposite of a diary: the fall seen from afterwards, as loss and as guilt for having survived.

sources.title: China Heritage: 1638, Zhang Dai in Nanking (tr. Duncan M. Campbell)
Jonathan Spence, AHA presidential address (2004) on Zhang Dai

eyes.name: Hayashi Gahō (林鵞峰, also Shunsai)
eyes.role: Confucian scholar to the Tokugawa shogunate, aged 26 in 1644; later compiler of the shogunate's China intelligence files
eyes.where: Edo, receiving reports gathered from Chinese ship captains at Nagasaki
eyes.authenticity: The 'Ka'i hentai' (華夷変態, 'The Transformation from Civilised to Barbarian') collects reports taken down from Chinese ship crews at Nagasaki from 1644 onward, compiled by Hayashi Gahō and his son. It is an administrative compilation, not a diary; the 1644 arrival of the news is dated here only to the month.
eyes.bio: Japan had cut itself off from the continent, and learned of China's catastrophe from sailors' depositions at Nagasaki. The title the Hayashi gave the file says how they read it: the civilised centre had fallen to barbarians. It is the view from furthest away, and the slowest.

sources.title: Samurai Archives: 1644 in Japan (Chinese merchants at Nagasaki report the fall of the Ming, Sept 1644)

entries.headline: At the founder's tomb, Zhang Dai sees a dark vapour
entries.digest: On a winter stay in Nanjing, Zhang lodged at a temple on Bell Mountain near the tomb of the Ming founder and noticed an ominous dark vapour hanging over it. He wrote this down only after the dynasty had fallen, so it is memory shaped by hindsight. Even so, it gives the mood of a capital of pleasure that did not yet know it was living through its last years.
entries.source_note: Tao'an mengyi, 'Bell Mountain', in Duncan Campbell's translation, China Heritage: https://chinaheritage.net/annual/2017/in-history/ming/earth-crumbles/1638-zhang-dai-in-nanking/

entries.headline: Rebels take the capital; the Jesuit refuses to run
entries.digest: Li Zicheng's Shun army entered Beijing and the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself on the hill behind the palace. Schall had been told by his superiors to leave the city for his own safety and refused, choosing to stay with the Christians of Beijing. His later account of these weeks was put together from letters years afterwards.
entries.source_note: Fall of Beijing 22–25 April 1644 (Jiashen Incident); Schall's refusal to leave: Chinese PEN profile, https://www.chinesepen.org/english/?p=1601

entries.headline: Dorgon marches south with the Grand Army
entries.digest: Dorgon left the Qing capital with the main army, heading for the Great Wall without yet knowing where he would strike. Within a week two officers from the Ming general Wu Sangui reached his camp asking for help against the rebels, and Dorgon answered the same day. The change of plan turned a raid into a conquest.
entries.source_note: Battle of Shanhai Pass (Wikipedia): departure 14 May, Wu's envoys 20 May; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Shanhai_Pass

entries.place: On the road south from Shenyang
entries.headline: The Korean hostage prince is taken along on the march
entries.digest: The prince's household diary for the 'northern journey' opens in the 4th lunar month of 1644, as the hostage heir and his retinue were made to travel with the Qing campaign. The diarists were Joseon officials, loyal in their hearts to the Ming, recording the movements of the army that would destroy it. The exact day of departure is dated here from Dorgon's march.
entries.source_note: Bukhaeng ilgi (4th–6th months 1644), AKS Encyclopedia of Korean Culture: https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0033853

entries.headline: News of the capital's fall reaches the south
entries.digest: The news that Beijing had fallen and the emperor was dead took weeks to travel down to Jiangnan, arriving by rumour, then by letter, in the 4th lunar month. Qi's 1644 diary volume belongs to these weeks of confusion, when officials in the south had to decide what they owed a dynasty with no emperor. The day and wording of his entries on the news are not verified here.
entries.source_note: Qi Biaojia riji runs continuously through 1644 (Zhang Tianjie, https://www.rujiazg.com/article/20824); timing of the news from standard chronologies

entries.headline: Wu Sangui opens the pass; the rebels are broken
entries.digest: Dorgon's army reached the gates of Shanhai Pass at dawn, Wu Sangui submitted, and the combined forces routed Li Zicheng's army that day. In his own pronouncements Dorgon cast the campaign as vengeance for the dead Ming emperor, not as conquest. Li fell back to Beijing and reached it four days later.
entries.source_note: Battle of Shanhai Pass (Wikipedia), 27 May 1644; Li back in Beijing 31 May; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Shanhai_Pass

entries.headline: The Korean retinue passes through the Great Wall's gate
entries.digest: The prince's party was with the Qing column as it went through the pass where the battle was fought. For Joseon men brought up on gratitude to the Ming for saving Korea in the 1590s, entering China behind a Manchu army was a bitter road. The journey diary is our window on how they saw it; its day-level content is not checked here.
entries.source_note: Bukhaeng ilgi coverage (AKS); battle date from the Qing campaign chronology

entries.headline: Li Zicheng crowns himself, then abandons the city
entries.digest: Back in Beijing after his defeat, Li Zicheng proclaimed himself emperor in the Wuying Palace and left the next day, setting fire to parts of the city as he went. Schall's household was among those that had lived through six weeks of Shun rule. His surviving narrative is retrospective; this entry gives the setting, not his words.
entries.source_note: Dates from the Battle of Shanhai Pass timeline (3–4 June); Schall's presence: NDB https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz77938.html

entries.headline: The Qing regent enters an emptied capital
entries.digest: Dorgon rode into Beijing, received by Ming officials who had expected Wu Sangui's restoration of the Ming. He ordered public mourning for the Chongzhen Emperor, presenting the Qing as avengers. He also ordered Chinese men to shave their foreheads in the Manchu way, an order that met such resistance that it was halted about a month later.
entries.source_note: Lunar 5/2 converts to 6 June (some English accounts give 5 June). Hair order halted 'just a month later': Tifayifu (Wikipedia), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tifayifu

entries.headline: A Korean hostage inside the Forbidden City's new masters' camp
entries.digest: The prince's party came into Beijing in the train of the conquerors. Korean envoys had come to the Ming capital for centuries as guests of the Son of Heaven; now Joseon's heir arrived as an attendant of the Manchu regent. The first stay was short, and the diary of the northern journey runs only to the 6th lunar month.
entries.source_note: Bukhaeng ilgi (4th–6th months 1644), AKS: https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0033853

entries.headline: Ordered out of the inner city, Schall stays put
entries.digest: The Manchus cleared Chinese residents out of large parts of the inner city to house their bannermen. Schall refused to abandon his residence and his library of some 3,000 books, and instead offered his services to the new dynasty. The gamble worked: he kept his house and gained a patron.
entries.source_note: Chinese PEN profile of Schall: refusal to move, offer of service, https://www.chinesepen.org/english/?p=1601

entries.headline: A new Ming emperor in the southern capital
entries.digest: Ming officials in Nanjing enthroned the Prince of Fu as the Hongguang Emperor. Shi Kefa, who had preferred another candidate, was sent north of the Yangtze to command the front around Yangzhou, away from court. The new regime hoped at first to ally with the Qing against the rebels.
entries.source_note: Southern Ming (Wikipedia): Hongguang enthroned 19 June 1644; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Ming

entries.headline: Qi Biaojia takes office for the southern court
entries.digest: Recalled to service by the Hongguang regime, Qi took up a senior regional post in Jiangnan, where the collapse of authority had loosed riots and score-settling against officials who had served the rebels. His diary for these months is that of a working administrator rather than a mourner. Within months, court factions around Ma Shiying pushed him out again.
entries.source_note: General outline of Qi's 1644 career; diary continuity per Zhang Tianjie (https://www.rujiazg.com/article/20824). Exact office and dates not verified here

entries.headline: Dorgon writes to Shi Kefa: submit
entries.digest: The regent sent a letter to Shi Kefa in the south demanding that the Southern Ming submit, arguing that the Qing had avenged the Ming emperor while the southerners had done nothing. The letter is a document of propaganda as much as diplomacy. Its exact date is given here only to the season.
entries.source_note: Shi Kefa (Wikipedia), 'Reply to Dorgon's letter'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Kefa

entries.headline: Schall's eclipse arrives on time
entries.digest: A solar eclipse had been forecast by three methods: the traditional Chinese, the Muslim, and Schall's European calculations. Schall's prediction matched the sky to the minute, the Chinese was off by about half an hour and the Muslim by about an hour. For a dynasty that needed to show Heaven was on its side, a calendar that worked was worth having.
entries.source_note: Chinese PEN profile: eclipse of 1 September 1644; https://www.chinesepen.org/english/?p=1601

entries.headline: Chinese sailors bring Japan word of the Ming's fall
entries.digest: Chinese merchants arriving at Nagasaki told the Japanese authorities that the Ming dynasty had fallen. Their depositions, sent up to Edo, began the file that Hayashi Gahō and his son later named 'the transformation from civilised to barbarian'. The news had taken about five months to arrive.
entries.source_note: Samurai Archives, 1644: 'September 1644: Chinese merchants in Nagasaki inform Japanese authorities of the fall of the Ming'; https://samurai-archives.com/wiki/1644

entries.headline: Shi Kefa answers Dorgon with a refusal
entries.digest: Shi replied to the regent's letter, thanking the Qing for defeating the rebels but refusing any submission and insisting on the legitimacy of the Hongguang Emperor. Later readers praised its tone as neither servile nor defiant. The reply changed nothing, and both sides prepared for war.
entries.source_note: Shi Kefa (Wikipedia): 'Reply to Dorgon's letter'; month not verified; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Kefa

entries.headline: With the Qing court, the prince moves to Beijing
entries.digest: When the Qing moved its capital from Shenyang to Beijing in the 9th lunar month, the hostage prince's household moved with it. The child Shunzhi Emperor arrived on 19 October and was enthroned on 8 November. Sohyeon spent about seventy days in the city.
entries.source_note: AKS (move to Yanjing in 9th month 1644); Shunzhi arrival 19 Oct and enthronement 8 Nov: Battle of Shanhai Pass article; 70 days: Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Prince_Sohyeon

entries.headline: The Jesuit and the Korean crown prince
entries.digest: Schall befriended Sohyeon during the prince's stay in Beijing, introducing him to Catholic teaching and Western science. The prince took Western books and objects home with him. Schall's own version of the friendship survives in his later narrative, so its warmth may be partly retrospective.
entries.source_note: Crown Prince Sohyeon (Wikipedia): met Schall in Beijing; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Prince_Sohyeon

entries.headline: Released at last, the hostage household heads home
entries.digest: In the 11th lunar month the Qing released the prince, ending eight years of captivity, and his party set out for Korea. The Shenyang diary's record of the hostage years ends here. A separate household diary covers the short months left to him in 1645.
entries.source_note: AKS: released and returned 11th month 1644; https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0033853; 1645 diary: https://kyeonggi.com/article/200607210192956

entries.headline: A foreigner heads the Qing Astronomical Bureau
entries.digest: Dorgon made Schall director of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau with mandarin rank. From 1645 the Qing issued its calendar on his methods, so the new dynasty began with a Jesuit's arithmetic in its official almanac. Schall would later face trial when that position became a target.
entries.source_note: NDB/ADB (appointment 1644 under Dorgon/Shunzhi), https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/sfz77938.html; Chinese PEN

entries.headline: Out of office, Qi retreats to his garden
entries.digest: Forced out of office by court factions, Qi went home to the Yushan garden he had spent years building and describing. His diary turns again to the garden, visitors and religious practice, which scholars read as a stage on which he watched the world. To the north, the Qing were preparing their drive on the Yangtze.
entries.source_note: Garden as 'theatre': Lin Zhu thesis abstract, https://era.ed.ac.uk/handle/1842/37694?show=full; Yushan garden: Masterworks note https://www.masterworks.com/academy/artists/qi-biaojia

entries.headline: The prince comes home to a cold welcome
entries.digest: Sohyeon reached Seoul in the 2nd lunar month of 1645, bringing Qing goodwill, Western books and new ideas. His father King Injo, who had been humiliated by the Qing in 1637, received him coldly. The household diary of 1645 records his last weeks.
entries.source_note: Hankyung (return February 1645); Crown Princess Minhoe and Crown Prince Sohyeon (Wikipedia); 1645 diary: Kyeonggi Ilbo, https://kyeonggi.com/article/200607210192956

entries.headline: Shi Kefa's army falls back; the gates are shut
entries.digest: Wang begins his record with the defeat of Shi Kefa's forces at the Baiyang River and their disordered retreat into Yangzhou. The city closed its gates against the approaching Qing army under Prince Dodo. Wang describes the soldiers billeted on households and the townspeople's growing fear.
entries.source_note: Yangzhou shiri ji, opening section (4th month, 14th day), East Asia Student: https://eastasiastudent.net/china/classical/yangzhou-shiri-ji-1/

entries.headline: Under siege, Shi Kefa writes his farewells
entries.digest: With the Qing army around Yangzhou and no relief coming, Shi wrote last letters to his mother, wife and family, expecting to die with the city. They are short and formal and resolved. Exact days of the letters are not verified here.
entries.source_note: Farewell letters in Shi Kefa's collected writings (Shi Zhongzheng gong ji); dates not verified

entries.headline: The city still holds, one more night
entries.digest: Wang notes that Yangzhou held out up to this day. In the same passage he tells of a banquet given by an officer named Yang and a letter from Shi Kefa that evening, signs that the defenders knew the end was close. It is the last evening of ordinary life in his account.
entries.source_note: Yangzhou shiri ji, section 1 (念四日), East Asia Student: https://eastasiastudent.net/china/classical/yangzhou-shiri-ji-1/

entries.headline: Yangzhou falls; Wang's family goes into hiding
entries.digest: The Qing broke into the city and the killing began. Wang moved his family from one hiding place to another, from rooftops to back rooms, and paid soldiers to let them go, again and again. Five members of his extended family were killed over the following days. He records what he saw without a historian's distance, and without exaggeration of his own suffering.
entries.source_note: Yangzhou shiri ji (4th month, 25th day onward); Wang Xiuchu (Wikipedia) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Xiuchu; Yangzhou massacre 20 May 1645, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangzhou_massacre

entries.headline: Shi Kefa is captured and killed
entries.digest: When the walls fell, Shi Kefa was taken and refused Dodo's offer to serve the Qing; he was executed. No writing of his survives from this day; we know his end mainly from witnesses such as Wang Xiuchu, whose account historians use to confirm it. His body was never identified, and a cenotaph of his clothes and cap stands in Yangzhou.
entries.source_note: Shi Kefa (Wikipedia), death 20 May 1645, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Kefa; Wang Xiuchu used to verify his death, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Xiuchu

entries.headline: Far to the east, the returned prince dies
entries.digest: The day after Yangzhou fell, Crown Prince Sohyeon died in Seoul, a few weeks after coming home, in circumstances that led many then and since to suspect poisoning. His 1645 household diary ends with his illness. King Injo passed over Sohyeon's sons and named his second son, the future Hyojong, as heir.
entries.source_note: Death 21 May 1645: Crown Prince Sohyeon (Wikipedia), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Prince_Sohyeon; 1645 diary: Kyeonggi Ilbo

entries.headline: The killing slackens, the looting does not
entries.digest: By the first day of the new month the slaughter had eased but not stopped. Soldiers still searched wealthy households, and a fresh unit came back into the city to take what was left. Wang and the survivors of his family were still hiding.
entries.source_note: Yangzhou shiri ji, section 18 (五月朔日), East Asia Student: https://eastasiastudent.net/china/classical/yangzhou-shiri-ji-18/

entries.headline: New officials, placards, and the burning of the dead
entries.digest: Qing officials were installed and placards posted to reassure the population. Monks were ordered to cremate the bodies piled in the streets, and Wang reports the cremation register as some 800,000, not counting those who drowned or killed themselves. Historians treat that number as a survivor's exaggeration; the city itself probably held no more than about 300,000 people.
entries.source_note: Yangzhou shiri ji, section 18 (初二), https://eastasiastudent.net/china/classical/yangzhou-shiri-ji-18/; population estimate (Struve, after Zhang Defang): Yangzhou massacre, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangzhou_massacre

entries.headline: Relief rice disappears in a moment
entries.digest: Relief grain was announced and Wang went with an old woman he was sheltering to the Quekou Gate, where rice from the army granary was handed out. It vanished almost at once, and the weak got nothing. The scene ends his record of the worst days: order restored, hunger unchanged.
entries.source_note: Yangzhou shiri ji, section 18 (初三), https://eastasiastudent.net/china/classical/yangzhou-shiri-ji-18/

entries.headline: Nanjing surrenders without a fight
entries.digest: Nanjing, the southern capital, opened its gates to Dodo, and the Hongguang Emperor fled and was soon captured. For Qi at his garden, the fall of Nanjing removed the last Ming government he had served. Scholars connect his final decision directly to this news.
entries.source_note: Nanjing surrender 8 June 1645 (Southern Ming, Wikipedia); his death 'when Nanjing fell' (Lin Zhu thesis abstract)

entries.headline: A monk's letter as the Qing army moves south
entries.digest: The 1645 diary records a letter from the Chan master Juelang Daosheng written while the Qing army was advancing into Zhejiang. Qi had long practised meditation and Buddhist-Confucian self-cultivation, and the diary of these weeks is partly a record of preparing his mind. Invitations to serve the new dynasty were coming to gentry like him.
entries.source_note: Qi Biaojia riji, vol. 15 'Yiyou rili', p. 829 (Zhang Tianjie ed. 2017), cited by Zhang Tianjie, https://www.rujiazg.com/article/20824

entries.headline: Shave the head or lose it: the queue order
entries.digest: With Nanjing taken, Dorgon reissued and now enforced the order that all Chinese men shave the front of the head and wear the Manchu queue, with short deadlines for submission once the order reached each place. Places that submitted without shaving were to be treated as wavering. The order, more than the conquest itself, set off uprisings across Jiangnan that summer.
entries.source_note: Day as commonly given in Chinese chronologies (Shunzhi 2, 6/15); content: Two Edicts (Schlager abstract) https://library.schlagergroup.com/chapter/9781961844254-book-part-010; Tifayifu (Wikipedia)

entries.date_display: Hongguang 1 / Shunzhi 2, intercalary 6th month, night of 5th–6th day (traditional)
entries.headline: Qi Biaojia walks into his garden pond
entries.digest: Rather than answer the Qing summons, Qi drowned himself at midnight in the water of his own garden, the place he had made into a stage, and was buried there in a coffin he had prepared. His diary runs up to his death. Accounts differ on the exact day and on details such as whether he fasted first.
entries.source_note: Lin Zhu thesis abstract (drowned at midnight in the garden lake after Nanjing fell), https://era.ed.ac.uk/handle/1842/37694?show=full; disagreement on date and setting: Masterworks, https://www.masterworks.com/academy/artists/qi-biaojia

entries.headline: Zhang Dai joins, then leaves, the Shaoxing resistance
entries.digest: After the Prince of Lu set up a Ming regency at Shaoxing, Zhang served briefly with the resistance. He withdrew his support, and local militarists looted and destroyed his property. It was the end of the wealth that had paid for the lanterns, opera troupes and tea he would later write about.
entries.source_note: Jonathan Spence, AHA presidential address, https://www.historians.org/presidential-address/jonathan-spence/

entries.headline: A red poster on the door as Wenzhou falls
entries.digest: As the Qing were about to take Wenzhou, Martini hung a large red notice saying that a teacher of the divine law from the Great West lived there, and set out European books, instruments and an altar beneath it. The Qing commander was impressed, asked if he would change sides, and Martini shaved his head, put on Qing dress, and was sent back to Hangzhou under protection. It is his own story, printed in some editions of his book.
entries.source_note: Martino Martini (Wikipedia), from Martini's own report; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martino_Martini

entries.headline: In hiding, Zhang Dai writes his dream memories
entries.digest: Poor and on the run, sheltering in monasteries and then in the hills south of Shaoxing, Zhang began writing short pieces recalling the world before 1644. In his preface he compares himself to a man waking from a dream. The collection was probably finished about 1647 and was not printed for over a century.
entries.source_note: Spence AHA address (https://www.historians.org/presidential-address/jonathan-spence/); completion c. 1647, first print 1775: China Heritage, https://chinaheritage.net/annual/2017/in-history/ming/earth-crumbles/1638-zhang-dai-in-nanking/

entries.headline: Europe reads the Tartar war
entries.digest: Martini's 'De bello Tartarico historia' was printed in Antwerp after his voyage to Europe. It went through about 25 editions in five languages by 1706, and gave European readers their picture of the conquest, including the suicides of Ming loyalists and the hair order. It mixes what he saw with what friends wrote to him.
entries.source_note: The Beijing Center library tour, https://thebeijingcenter.org/cultural-dialogues/library-tour-eyewitness-to-the-fall-of-the-ming-dynasty-part-1/; Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martino_Martini

convergences.label: Beijing falls and the news begins to travel
convergences.note: Schall was inside the city the day it fell; Qi in Jiangnan heard only weeks later; Hayashi's Japan heard about five months later, from sailors. Reading them together shows how slowly a change of dynasty actually reached people.

convergences.label: Shanhai Pass
convergences.note: The conqueror's own words present the battle as vengeance for the Ming; the Korean hostages travelling with his army, still loyal to the Ming at heart, saw it as an outsider's catastrophe.

convergences.label: The Qing enter Beijing
convergences.note: Three foreigners to the Ming city in one week: the Manchu regent taking it, the Korean prince brought in behind him, and the German Jesuit deciding to stay and serve.

convergences.label: Late summer 1644: letters and signs
convergences.note: As Schall's eclipse showed the Qing could read Heaven, Dorgon's letter and Shi Kefa's reply settled that north and south would fight, and Japan was only now hearing the Ming had fallen.

convergences.label: Yangzhou falls; Sohyeon dies the next day in Seoul
convergences.note: On 20–21 May 1645 the Ming's most famous defender was killed at Yangzhou and the Korean prince who had marched with the conquerors died at home. Wang's account is the main witness to Shi's end.

convergences.label: The queue order and the loyalist's choice
convergences.note: Dorgon's order made submission visible on every man's head; a few weeks later Qi chose death over answering the new dynasty. Their writings face each other directly.

convergences.label: Zhejiang under conquest
convergences.note: Two men in the same province took opposite paths: the Jesuit shaved his head and survived with honour, the Shaoxing aesthete lost everything and survived with guilt, and both wrote it up afterwards.

ties.note: Schall befriended the crown prince in Beijing in autumn 1644, introducing him to Catholic teaching and Western science; the prince took books and objects back to Korea.
Dorgon wrote to Shi Kefa demanding submission in 1644; Shi's reply refused, and a year later Dorgon's brother Dodo besieged and took his city.
Both inside Yangzhou during the siege; Wang mentions a letter from Shi on the last night, and his account is used by historians to confirm Shi's death.
Friends and fellow Shaoxing gentlemen who had worked together on famine relief; one wrote a diary to the end and died with the Ming, the other survived and wrote memories.
Fellow Jesuits on opposite ends of the conquest: Schall serving the Qing in Beijing from 1644, Martini serving the Southern Ming until 1646; both shaped how Europe understood the change.
Dorgon let Schall keep his house, gave him rank, and put him in charge of the Astronomical Bureau.
The Korean hostage was taken along on the regent's campaign; captor and captive travelled to Beijing together.
Martini's book told Europe about the Manchu conquest and the hair order that Dorgon decreed.

threads_out.note: Joseon's loyalty to the Ming rested on gratitude for the Ming armies sent to Korea against Hideyoshi in 1592–98. That debt made the 1637 submission to the Qing and Sohyeon's eight hostage years especially bitter, and coloured how his diarists saw the Ming's fall.

Wang Xiuchu's Yangzhou account was suppressed under the Qing and reprinted by anti-Qing revolutionaries before 1911, making Yangzhou the classic remembered massacre of the lower Yangtze. In modern Chinese memory it is often set beside Nanjing 1937; the 1645 surrender of Nanjing itself spared that city a sack.

The Ka'i hentai began the Tokugawa practice of collecting foreign news from ship crews at Nagasaki. The same channel, through Dutch reports, warned Edo of the American expedition before Perry arrived in 1853.
The dynasty that Dorgon installed in 1644, with the queue as the sign of loyalty, is the Qing that fought Britain in 1839–42.
